questions.q: A leaf in bright light takes in 30 cm³ of carbon dioxide from the air each hour. In the same conditions, the leaf's respiration releases 8 cm³ of carbon dioxide each hour. What is the gross rate at which photosynthesis fixes carbon dioxide?
options: 38 cm³ of carbon dioxide per hour
22 cm³ of carbon dioxide per hour
30 cm³ of carbon dioxide per hour
8 cm³ of carbon dioxide per hour
questions.explanation: The 30 cm³ per hour taken in from the air is the net uptake. To find the gross rate, add the carbon dioxide released by respiration: 30 + 8 = 38 cm³ per hour. Subtracting 8 would incorrectly reduce the amount fixed rather than account for the carbon dioxide from respiration.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes respiration from breathing?
options: Respiration only occurs when oxygen is absent, while breathing supplies oxygen to the lungs.
Respiration is the movement of air into and out of the lungs; breathing is a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose.
Respiration is the exchange of gases between the blood and the alveoli; breathing is the breakdown of glucose in cells.
Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose; breathing is the movement of air into and out of the lungs.
questions.explanation: Respiration is the controlled release of energy from glucose in cells, while breathing is a mechanical process that moves air. Gas exchange in the lungs supports respiration but is not the same process.

questions.q: In a leaf, carbon dioxide enters through stomata and moves to the chloroplasts in the palisade cells. Which feature of the leaf's internal structure most directly speeds up this movement through the leaf?
options: Xylem vessels carrying water to the leaf
Large air spaces between the spongy mesophyll cells
A thick waxy cuticle on the upper surface
Many chloroplasts in the palisade cells
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide diffuses through the air spaces between spongy mesophyll cells before reaching photosynthesising cells. The waxy cuticle reduces water loss, whereas chloroplasts and xylem are not mainly involved in moving carbon dioxide through the leaf.

questions.q: In fruit flies, the allele for normal wings (W) is dominant to the allele for curled wings (w). Two heterozygous normal-wing flies are crossed. What is the probability that an offspring has curled wings?
questions.explanation: The cross is Ww × Ww. The possible offspring genotypes are WW, Ww, Ww and ww, so only ww has curled wings: 1 out of 4, or 25%. A 75% result would be the probability of normal wings.

questions.q: In a reflex arc, which neurone carries an electrical impulse between a sensory neurone and a motor neurone?
options: Sensory neurone
Effector neurone
Relay neurone
Motor neurone
questions.explanation: A relay neurone lies in the central nervous system and connects sensory input to motor output. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors, and motor neurones carry impulses to effectors.

questions.q: Mayfly nymphs are sensitive to water pollution. A student finds many mayfly nymphs in a stream. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The water is acidic because of sulfur dioxide in the air.
The water contains a high concentration of nitrate fertiliser.
The water is clean and well oxygenated.
The water is low in oxygen and heavily polluted.
questions.explanation: Mayfly nymphs need high oxygen levels and are intolerant of pollution, so many of them indicate clean, well-oxygenated water. Bloodworms and rat-tailed maggots, for example, are more likely to be found in polluted or low-oxygen water.

questions.q: Why are decomposers important in an ecosystem?
options: They convert carbon dioxide in the air into glucose for other organisms.
They remove all bacteria and fungi from the soil so plants can grow.
They transfer energy directly from dead material to plants during photosynthesis.
They break down dead material and release mineral ions that plants can absorb.
questions.explanation: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, digest dead organic matter and release mineral ions into the soil for plant uptake. They also release carbon dioxide by respiration, but they do not carry out photosynthesis or supply energy directly to plants.

questions.q: A patient called Grace has a section of her small intestine removed during surgery. Which function of the digestive system is most directly reduced by this operation?
options: Absorption of digested nutrients into the blood
Absorption of most remaining water from undigested food
Production of bile to emulsify fats
Chewing and physical breakdown of food in the mouth
questions.explanation: The small intestine is the main site of absorption of digested nutrients; its folded lining and villi provide a large surface area and a rich blood supply. Bile is produced by the liver, chewing occurs in the mouth, and most remaining water is absorbed in the large intestine, so removing part of the small intestine does not directly reduce those processes.

questions.q: Nia from Swansea looks at a cross-section of a plant stem. Which tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to other parts of the plant?
options: Palisade mesophyll tissue
Xylem tissue
Phloem tissue
Epidermal tissue
questions.explanation: Phloem tissue carries dissolved sugars, such as sucrose, made in the leaves to roots, stems and growing parts. Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions upwards, while epidermal tissue covers the plant and palisade mesophyll tissue is the main site of photosynthesis in leaves.

questions.q: The trachea is lined with ciliated epithelial tissue. Which statement best describes the main function of this tissue?
options: It sweeps mucus, dust and microorganisms away from the lungs.
It exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood.
It produces antibodies that destroy pathogens.
It strengthens the trachea and keeps it open.
questions.explanation: Cilia are tiny hair-like structures that beat to move mucus, which traps dust and microorganisms, away from the lungs. Gas exchange occurs in the alveoli, cartilage keeps the trachea open, and antibodies are produced by white blood cells, not ciliated epithelial tissue.

questions.q: A sperm cell has many mitochondria in the mid-piece. Which statement best explains why this adaptation is useful?
options: The mitochondria make antibodies to protect the sperm.
The mitochondria store genetic material for the offspring.
The mitochondria increase water uptake to keep the sperm hydrated.
The mitochondria release energy for the tail to move.
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which transfers energy for the sperm tail to contract and swim towards the egg. They do not contain the genetic material, produce antibodies or mainly absorb water.

questions.q: A single-celled organism such as Amoeba has no specialised gas exchange surface. Which statement best explains why oxygen can reach all parts of its cytoplasm by diffusion?
options: It uses active transport to move oxygen into its cells.
It has a transport system that carries oxygen around its body.
It has a small surface area compared with its volume.
It has a large surface area compared with its volume.
questions.explanation: A single-celled organism is very small, so its surface area to volume ratio is large; oxygen diffuses in quickly enough to supply the whole cell. A transport system is not needed, and oxygen moves by diffusion rather than active transport.

questions.q: Aoife in Belfast falls and cuts her knee. Which statement best explains why the cut increases the risk of infection?
options: The cut reduces the number of white blood cells in the body.
The cut breaks the skin barrier, allowing pathogens to enter the body.
The cut causes the body to produce fewer memory cells.
The cut makes antibiotics less effective against bacteria.
questions.explanation: Intact skin is a non-specific barrier that prevents many pathogens from entering the body. A cut creates a break in this barrier, so microorganisms can enter the wound and potentially cause infection; it does not directly reduce white blood cells, memory cells or antibiotic effectiveness.

questions.q: Some bacteria release toxins that cause disease symptoms. Which statement describes the role of antitoxins in the immune response?
options: They help blood clot at the site of infection.
They are antibiotics that kill bacteria directly.
They neutralise the toxins released by the pathogens.
They engulf bacteria by phagocytosis.
questions.explanation: Antitoxins are produced by white blood cells and bind to toxins, neutralising them so they cannot cause harm. Engulfing pathogens is phagocytosis, clotting involves platelets, and antibiotics are medicines rather than substances made by the immune system.

questions.q: Which of these human characteristics normally shows continuous variation?
options: Ability to roll the tongue
Hand span
Presence or absence of free earlobes
ABO blood group
questions.explanation: Continuous variation varies across a range with no distinct categories, such as hand span measured in centimetres. ABO blood group, tongue rolling and earlobe attachment are usually placed in discrete categories controlled mainly by genes.

questions.q: On a sandy beach, a population of mice has either light fur or dark fur. Birds of prey catch dark mice more often than light mice. Over many generations, the proportion of mice with light fur increases. Which statement best explains this increase?
options: Light-furred mice are more likely to survive and reproduce, so the allele for light fur becomes more common in the population.
Individual dark-furred mice change their fur colour to light during their lifetime.
Mice with dark fur grow more slowly and produce fewer offspring because of the colour of the sand.
The birds of prey create a new allele for light fur in the mice.
questions.explanation: The birds act as a selection pressure: light-furred mice are camouflaged and survive to pass on alleles. A new allele is not caused by predation; selection changes the frequency of existing variation.

questions.q: A normal human female produces egg cells. Which sex chromosome arrangement is found in a normal egg cell?
options: One Y chromosome
Two X chromosomes
One X or one Y chromosome
One X chromosome
questions.explanation: Egg cells are formed by meiosis in a female, who has two X chromosomes in her body cells, so each egg receives one X chromosome. A Y chromosome is passed in sperm from a male.

questions.q: On a hot day, a person's body temperature begins to rise. Which pair of responses helps the body to lose heat?
options: Sweat glands produce less sweat, and skin arterioles narrow.
Shivering starts, and hairs on the skin stand up.
Sweat glands produce more sweat, and skin arterioles widen.
Muscle cells take up more glucose, and the breathing rate falls.
questions.explanation: More sweat increases evaporation from the skin, which transfers heat energy to the surroundings. Widening skin arterioles increases blood flow near the surface, so more heat is lost by radiation and convection.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a reflex action?
options: A voluntary movement planned in the brain.
A rapid, automatic response that does not require a conscious decision.
A response that only occurs after a person learns it.
A slow response coordinated by hormones carried in the blood.
questions.explanation: Reflex actions are involuntary and fast, helping to protect the body, such as pulling a hand away from a hot object. The spinal cord or brain coordinates the response without waiting for conscious thought, while learned and hormonal responses work differently.

questions.q: A farmer wants to increase the biodiversity of the farm. Which change is most likely to achieve this?
options: Spray the field margins with a broad-spectrum herbicide.
Drain a pond so the land can be used for crops.
Plant a variety of native hedges and trees around the field margins.
Grow the same crop over every field each year.
questions.explanation: A range of native plants provides more habitats and food sources for different organisms. Removing hedges, spraying herbicides or draining ponds usually reduces the variety of species present.

questions.q: In a lake, two species of fish feed on different sizes of water flea. One feeds on small water fleas near the surface and the other on larger water fleas near the bottom. How does this reduce competition between the species?
options: They both have exactly the same niche but avoid each other by migrating.
They interbreed so they become one species.
They occupy slightly different niches, using different food sizes and areas of the lake.
One species preys on the other species.
questions.explanation: Using different parts of the habitat and different food sizes means the two species do not compete for exactly the same resources. This is a form of niche separation that allows them to coexist.

questions.q: A population of rabbits is introduced to an island with no predators and plenty of grass. After several years, the population stops increasing and then stays roughly constant. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Competition for food and space increases, and disease may spread more easily as the population becomes crowded.
Every rabbit becomes too old to reproduce at the same time.
The rabbits stop reproducing because each rabbit needs less food.
The grass grows faster each year without any limit.
questions.explanation: As population density rises, resources such as food and space become limiting, and disease is more likely to spread. These factors increase death rate or reduce birth rate, so the population size levels off rather than continuing to grow.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the function of muscular tissue in the wall of the stomach?
options: It secretes bile to break down fats.
It carries oxygenated blood away from the heart.
It absorbs most of the digested glucose into the blood.
It contracts to churn food and mix it with digestive juices.
questions.explanation: The stomach is an organ with muscular tissue that contracts to mechanically break up food and mix it with acid and enzymes. Absorption of most digested glucose occurs in the small intestine, bile is made in the liver, and arteries carry blood away from the heart.

questions.q: Which feature of an artery is most closely related to carrying blood at high pressure?
options: Valves along its length that stop blood flowing backwards.
A thick muscular wall containing elastic fibres.
A wall that is one cell thick to shorten the diffusion distance.
A very wide lumen with very little muscle in the wall.
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so a thick, muscular and elastic wall helps withstand pressure and stretch then recoil. Thin walls suit capillaries for exchange, valves are typical of veins, and a wide lumen with little muscle is suited to veins rather than arteries.

questions.q: A student views a root hair cell using a light microscope. Which structure is present in the cell but is normally too small to be seen clearly with this type of microscope?
options: Vacuole
Cell wall
Ribosome
Nucleus
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are about 20 nm across, which is below the resolution of a light microscope, so they cannot be seen clearly. The cell wall, nucleus and large vacuole are much larger and can be seen with a light microscope.

questions.q: A cube-shaped model cell has sides of length 2 mm. What is its surface area to volume ratio, written as surface area:volume in its simplest whole-number form?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 × (2 mm × 2 mm) = 24 mm²; volume = 2 mm × 2 mm × 2 mm = 8 mm³. The ratio is 24:8, which simplifies to 3:1. Writing 1:3 would reverse the ratio as volume:surface area.

questions.q: Which defence mechanism is non-specific, meaning it acts against many pathogens rather than one particular antigen?
options: White blood cells releasing antitoxins after recognising a toxin.
Sticky mucus in the airways trapping microorganisms.
Memory cells responding rapidly after a second infection.
Antibodies binding to antigens on a pathogen.
questions.explanation: Mucus in the airways traps microorganisms as a physical barrier and is not directed at one particular antigen. Antibodies, memory cells and antitoxins are part of responses that recognise specific antigens or toxins.

questions.q:
A student measures the volume of oxygen released by pondweed in 10 minutes at different temperatures. Light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration are constant.
Temperature: 5 °C, 15 °C, 25 °C, 35 °C
Oxygen released in 10 minutes/cm³: 3, 9, 12, 4
Which statement best explains the results?
options: The rate rises up to 25 °C as enzyme activity increases, but at 35 °C some photosynthetic enzymes are denatured.
At 35 °C photosynthesis has stopped completely, so all the oxygen released comes from respiration.
The rate rises continuously with temperature because increasing temperature always increases the rate of photosynthesis.
The rate at 5 °C is highest because enzymes are less likely to denature in cold water.
questions.explanation: The highest value is 12 cm³ at 25 °C, so the rate rises from 5 °C to 25 °C as enzyme activity increases. At 35 °C the rate falls to 4 cm³ because some enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured, changing the shape of their active sites.

questions.q: A student puts equal masses of live germinating seeds, boiled seeds that have been cooled, and dry seeds into separate insulated tubes for 24 hours. Which tube is expected to show the greatest temperature rise, and why?
options: The tube with dry seeds, because without water they respire fastest.
All three tubes equally, because seeds are at the same starting temperature.
The tube with boiled seeds, because boiling breaks down stored starch into glucose and releases heat.
The tube with live germinating seeds, because respiration releases energy and some is transferred as heat.
questions.explanation: Live germinating seeds respire, breaking down stored glucose and releasing energy; some of this energy is transferred as heat. Boiled seeds are dead and dry seeds are dormant, so neither respires enough to produce the same temperature rise.

questions.q: Which characteristic is an example of variation caused only by genes in a person?
options: Body mass
ABO blood group
The language a person speaks
A scar
questions.explanation: Blood group is determined by inherited alleles, so it is an example of genetic variation. Body mass is affected by diet and exercise, a scar is caused by the environment, and spoken language is learned.
